title: First Nations health watchdog investigating how Sask. boy lost use of small intestine after routine surgery
summary: Saskatchewan's First Nations Health Ombudsperson is investigating how a Regina boy lost his small intestine after a routine surgery for appendicitis.

image.caption: First Nations Health Ombudsperson Dianne Lafond, right, and Kristen Lerat, centre, speak to media in Saskatoon on Wednesday. (Chanss Lagaden/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New
Saskatchewan's First Nations Health Ombudsperson is investigating how a Regina boy lost his small intestine after a routine surgery for appendicitis.
Sask. Health Authority also conducting internal review
Saskatchewan's First Nations Health Ombudsperson is investigating how a Regina boy lost the use of his small intestine after a routine surgery for appendicitis.
Sheldon OneBear Rosebluff, 4, is now in critical condition at the Jim Pattison Children's Hospital in Saskatoon. He requires a small intestine transplant.
On Wednesday, his family and First Nations leaders held a media event to discuss the case and ongoing concerns about how Indigenous people are treated by the provincial health-care system.

First Nations Health Ombudsperson Dianne Lafond said she launched an investigation into Rosebluff's medical ordeal after the boy's family filed a complaint. Lafond said she can't discuss the details of Rosebluff's situation until the investigation is complete.

"Nothing is black and white and some cases are very complex," Lafond said on Wednesday. "When a child goes in for a simple procedure and will now be in the health-care system for years … you've got a lot of different factors at play."
The Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA) confirmed it is conducting its own review of the care Rosebluff received in hospital.

items: FSIN appoints ombudsperson to investigate racism in health care

blocks.text: Kristin Lerat is Rosebluff's biological aunt and has been his caregiver for about three years. She described Rosebluff as a talkative boy who likes to build forts, dance and drum.
"A happy, energized boy. And this has taken the richness out of not only his life, but our lives too," Lerat said.
In September, Rosebluff had a successful surgery in Regina for appendicitis. He appeared to be recovering well until Oct. 24, when he suddenly turned ill and was taken back to hospital, Lerat said.

He had a blockage in his bowels and required surgery. After two surgeries in Regina within days, he was airlifted to Jim Pattison Children's Hospital in Saskatoon, where he eventually had two more surgeries over the course of a week.
"He was critical the whole time, but his body just couldn't handle that many surgeries," Lerat said.
Something happened that "killed" his small intestine and he now requires a transplant, Lerat said.
Sheldon One Bear Rosebluff, 4, seen here in an undated photo prior to his medical ordeal. (Submitted by Kristen Lerat)
The SHA declined to comment on Rosebluff surgeries and his condition due to privacy legislation.
But the SHA is conducting a review of the care Rosebluff received and "what might have occured," according to a statement emailed to CBC.

"Patient safety and the delivery of high-quality, patient-centred care remain top priorities for the SHA, and we take patient safety concerns very seriously," SHA chief medical officer Dr. Rashaad Hansia said in the statement.

"Social Work supports are in place to assist in liaising with the family and coordinating with partner agencies, and we are commit[ted] to ensuring these interactions and supports are provided in a culturally respectful way."
Lafond did not provided a timeline for the ombudsperson investigation, but said more details will be released once it is complete.
Cowessess First Nation Chief Erica Beaudin attended the media event to support the Lerat family.
"We are not here to denounce the health-care system or the people in it," Beaudin said.
"What we're talking about is how we must recognize when we must do better.… For us, treaty is not a land acknowledgement. It is action."
The First Nations Health Ombudsperson is an independent office established by the Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations to investigate complaints about the health-care system.

In October 2025, the ombudsperson said her office had received about 500 complaints since opening in 2023. About 64 per cent of the cases derived from complaints and issues associated with the services of the Saskatchewan Health Authority.

The boy's family is also concerned about being sidelined for important medical decisions. Lerat said the social services ministry took over decision-making for Rosebluff's care once the boy's condition turned critical.

"It was me and the doctors making the decisions. Now it's the ministries and the doctors making decisions," Lerat said. "So if we get a doctor that does not believe in our traditional ways, what does that look like?"
The Ministry of Social Services provided a statement to CBC.
"Due to provisions in The Child and Family Services Act, the Ministry of Social Services is unable to confirm involvement with a family or speak to specific details of any case," it said.
